pending_items.title: Iran rations electricity: How deeply are US sanctions, blockade biting?
pending_items.content:
Wearing a blue jacket to protect against the cold, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian pores over paperwork under a table lamp in his dimly lit office as he asks millions of Iranians to conserve electricity as an energy crisis compounds the country’s economic battering.

During a televised interview with state broadcaster IRIB at the presidential office on Tehran’s Pasteur Street, the chandeliers are switched off and curtains drawn aside to let in daylight instead.

Tehran controls one part of the world’s largest natural gasfield and has the world’s third-largest proven oil reserves. But millions of Iranians are now rationing electricity as the authorities impose rolling power cuts from Sunday, expected to last for about two hours every day.

Iran has been consistent in its refusal to bow to Washington’s demands for ending the war, which is currently at an impasse. But after months of a US naval blockade against Iranian ports – aggravated by biting sanctions and strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure – its economy is reeling, and a punishing winter looms amid an escalating energy crisis.

So, how deeply are US sanctions and the blockade biting the Iranian economy?

Iran was suffering gas shortages and power cuts before the United States and Israel jointly attacked Tehran and nuclear facilities across the country on February 28. Strikes since then have targeted other energy, military and civilian facilities .

Fatemeh Mohajerani, a government spokeswoman, warned last week that Iran’s gas shortfall could reach 430 million cubic metres a day this winter, compared with about 300 million in previous years.

National Iranian Gas Company managing director Saeed Tavakoli said this month ‌that four processing plants had been damaged during the first phase of the conflict early this year, which initially reduced capacity by 230 million cubic metres, of which about 100 million had so far been restored.

Last week, the company warned that 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces ⁠could face supply difficulties this winter, in particular Mazandaran on the Caspian Sea, and Golestan and North Khorasan along Iran’s border with Turkmenistan.

“Given the country’s fuel supply conditions, the electricity sector will be forced to impose distribution restrictions from Sunday,” Mohammad Allahdad, head of Iran’s national electricity company Tavanir, told state TV, as he announced the power cuts.

Iran operates hundreds of power plants which, together, form one of the largest electricity systems in the Middle East, supplying energy to 92 million people.

Pezeshkian told ISNA news agency that “the attack on the country’s gas infrastructure has aggravated the situation and we should therefore expect difficulties this winter”.

Separately, Pezeshkian told a group of investors and producers on November 21 that Iran is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles,” the state news agency IRNA has reported.

An Al Jazeera analysis of Iran’s power grid shows that about 86 percent of the country’s electricity is usually generated from natural gas supplies. Some gas-fired power stations switch to diesel or fuel oil when natural gas supplies are tight, especially during winter demand peaks.

Oil-fired plants provide a smaller share, generating roughly 7 percent of the nation’s electricity.

Hydropower accounts for about 5 percent of electricity. Nuclear energy contributes about 2 percent of the country’s electricity, mainly from the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, Iran’s only operational nuclear reactor.

Earlier in August, Iran’s Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi told reporters that Iran’s power plants lost 4,200 megawatts of generation capacity in war-related attacks and repairs were under way.

But shortages of fuel to fire up the plants are worsening as well.

“Energy imbalance was also a serious issue in Iran even before these wars,” said Iranian economist Mohammad Reza Farzanegan, a professor at Philipps-Universitat Marburg in Germany.

“Higher energy consumption driven by subsidised prices, waste, inefficiencies, and mismanagement could not be met with a proportional increase in energy production due to a lack of investment under sanctions, and now wars,” he told Al Jazeera.

In the years before the current war, Farzanegan said he identified “fragmented governance, structural inefficiencies, and price distortions as the key drivers of chronic energy insecurity in Iran”.

Electricity shortages have also resulted in about 600,000 job losses because of the reduction of industrial production during the US-Israel war, politicians say.

Parliamentarian Nasrollah Pejmanfar told the Khaneh Mellat News Agency (ICANA) on November 21 that more than one million workers could lose their jobs if natural gas shortages continue.

The Trump administration claims that its Operation Economic Outcast – measures it has taken to strangle Iran’s economy by sanctioning those who do business with Iran – will force concessions from an otherwise unrelenting Tehran. Iran itself has already been the subject of sanctions by the US and other nations for decades.

On the ground, that has made the lives of millions of Iranians worse.

For the seventh Iranian month of Mehr (September 23 to October 22), Iran’s 12-month average annual inflation rate was 76.8 percent, according to the Statistical Centre of Iran. Point-to-point inflation, which compares that month with the same month of the previous year, was at 88.7 percent.

Essential goods have already been subject to triple-digit inflation for months, with food, beverages and tobacco experiencing year-on-year inflation of 113.4 percent in October, the centre said.

“The real gross domestic product of Iran is expected to experience significant negative growth in 2026 (about -7 percent) compared to 2025, which was also just below 0 percent,” added economist Farzanegan.

“This is the sharpest contraction in the Iranian economy since the end of the Iran-Iraq War, and it represents a steeper decline than earlier sanction episodes after 2012,” he told Al Jazeera.

The reasons are, he argued, “more intense sanctions combined with a physical trade embargo, war damage, and the resulting economic uncertainty and higher business risks”.

The ongoing US naval blockade on Iranian ports, which has dealt a blow to Iran’s oil revenues , Farzanegan said, is now confronting “the government with budget deficits because, despite lower revenues, government expenditures have not declined proportionally; for example, it is hard to cut large energy subsidies or increase tax revenues under such political conditions”.

Without a relaxation of sanctions and renewed access to global investment and finance, there is little it can do, analysts say.

Last week, several Iranian officials, including Pezeshkian, said the government was working to prevent power cuts this winter. Nonetheless, the announcement that they will take place came this week.

While Pezeshkian can turn off lights at the presidential office in Tehran to send a symbolic message, two-hour power cuts scheduled from Sunday may not be enough, Farzanegan said. “If the blockade continues, these inflationary pressures will increase,” he added.

While changes in consumer behaviour are helpful for saving energy, he argued, “the real driver of that behaviour is energy cost”.

To address the energy imbalance, Farzanegan said, Iran needs to reduce the energy intensity of production, which requires the lifting of US and other sanctions, access to finance, and long-term planning. Then, an increase in energy efficiency of consumption requires investment in new production and consumption technologies alongside subsidy reforms, he added.

pending_items.title: Could Netanyahu take Israel into another war with Iran to cling to power?
pending_items.content:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot is seeking to form a coalition government before an escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran works to interim Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s advantage.

Eisenkot’s bloc’s 48 seats still leave him 13 short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset needed to form a new government. But he could count on the support of the Arab parties and their 19 seats from outside the government, which could be enough to cross the line.

Netanyahu’s supporters are averse to an alliance with the Arab parties, while the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance could support either side in the coalition talks.

The Netanyahu-led Likud party’s 46 recommendations from Knesset members following UTJ’s decision not to endorse either candidate could prove decisive ahead of the initial December 6 deadline for a government to be formed.

Negotiations between Eisenkot’s Yashar (“Straight”) party and Likud remain fractious. Eisenkot has already ruled out serving in any government led by Netanyahu, but has pressed for a unity government where he would share leadership roles with another party leader.

Netanyahu argues that Israel needs a government free from what he portrays as the “taint” of Arab-party participation and can respond to what he has argued is an imminent military threat from Iran.

Some analysts argue that renewed conflict with Iran could derail negotiations, forcing the rival blocs to fall in line behind Netanyahu .

But Eisenkot has told party members he has seen no imminent threat requiring military action before a new government is sworn in. His ally, Avigdor Liberman, recently appointed to the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee and therefore privy to classified intelligence, also said he had seen no justifications for new Israeli strikes.

“If we end up seeing a strike right now, then we’ll know that it’s completely motivated by politics and not security concerns,” Liberman told Israeli media.

Israel’s military chief, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir, and researchers within Mossad, the country’s foreign intelligence service, also reportedly see no case for an immediate attack on Iran.

Although defence officials have warned Netanyahu that new attacks on Iran could trigger a wider regional conflict, Mossad chief Roman Gofman has reportedly advocated for renewed military action.

So, how pressing is the case for war, and could it really override negotiations to form government?

In mid-November, US media reported that Netanyahu dispatched his longstanding ally Gofman to Washington, DC, to urge joint strikes on Iran, based on new intelligence Israel had reportedly uncovered indicating that Tehran was developing chemical weapons.

Several other Netanyahu appointees are also reported to support military action. On Tuesday , Netanyahu’s decades-old ally, Defence Minister Israel Katz, called for preemptive strikes against Iran before it could fully develop the chemical weapons programme he claimed was already under way.

Also reportedly backing new strikes on Iran is David Zini , head of the Shin Bet internal security agency, and two further Netanyahu appointees – National Security Council chair Shmuel Ben Ezra and Israel’s ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter.

US President Donald Trump appeared to echo many of Netanyahu’s claims in a November 19 interview Fox News on, although he stopped short of committing to military action before the end of the year.

“There is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear. Nuclear is much harder. And they’re looking at gas and… biological weapons, not nice, and other things,” he said, without providing evidence.

Gulf countries, which would likely be heavily affected by a renewed conflict with Iran, have reportedly urged Washington to maintain its economic pressure on Tehran rather than return to military action. According to the US news website Axios , some senior US officials are also highly sceptical of Israel’s claims, with one telling the outlet they appeared to be “driven by an agenda”.

Iran has also denied developing chemical weapons, and has compared claims that it is with the false claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, used to justify the US-led invasion in 2003.

Writing on X, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei accused those making the allegations of expecting the world to suffer “a bout of collective amnesia”, likening the situation to Dory, the forgetful fish from the 2003 animated film Finding Nemo.

Many in Israel regard Iran as the ultimate regional threat. For years, Iranian propaganda and that of its regional allies, such as Hezbollah in Lebanon, have called for the destruction of Israel as a state. There have also been repeated claims by Netanyahu, dating back to at least the 1990s, that Iran is poised to develop a nuclear weapon that could be deployed against Israel without hesitation.

“If war started, even manufactured, everyone would rally around the flag, as this is what Israelis do in crisis,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said.

“Netanyahu can go to war knowing that no political leader will oppose him the moment bombs started falling on Iran,” he said.

Netanyahu has been frequently accused of prioritising his political survival over other pressing national issues, and some believe he could restart the war on Iran to save his career.

Alongside the multiple corruption charges for which he has been on trial since 2020 are allegations that he misled lawmakers about his administration’s failures ahead of the October 7 Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, sparking Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, to stave off an inquiry.

There have also been widespread accusations, including from former US President Joe Biden, that Netanyahu has prolonged the genocide in Gaza for political reasons.

“I think it would be very easy for him,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flashenberg said.

“His own survival and what he sees as Israel’s are aligned. It’s not that he thinks of it purely in terms of attacking Iran to stay in office. He sees attacking Iran, as he always has, as necessary for Israel and a path that will also need him to stay in office.”
